110 THIRTY-SIXTH REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
August 6, 1919. 
Mrs. A. D. Miller may be appointed to a clerical position in the Department of Commerce without reference to the civil-service rules. Mrs. Miller is the wife of A. D. Miller, an employee of the Bureau of Standards, who has recently suffered a.complete nervous breakdown, brought about by the jcransed volume of work which he was handling due to the war activities of that 
ureat. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce who . states that there are positions in the Department of Commerce in which Mrs, Miller could be employed to good advantage. 
August 9, 1919. 
Mrs. K. E. Bollinger may be reinstated in the classified service without regard to the year limitation as prescribed by the civil-service rules. Mrs. Bollinger (formerly Miss Katherine E. Schwartz) was employed for about 16 years in the Post Office Department, Division of Dead Letters, She was transferred to Fort Wayne, Ind., January 1, 1914, reinstated to a clerkship in the Cleveland, Ohio, post office on June 10, 1914, and resigned September 30, 1917, to be married. Her husband, who was employed as.a clerk in the Cleveland office for about 27 years, died March 1, 1919, leaving his widow without means of support. In view of the long and efficient service rendered by Mrs. Bollinger, and her knowl- edge of post office work, this order is issued upon the recommendation of the Post- master General. The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this order. 
August 12, 1919. 
Mr. Ira F. Hoyt may be appointed to the position of passport agent, New York 
City, under the Department of State without reference to the civil-service law. This order is issued because of the difficulty of securing a competent and experi- enced man for the position through the usual civil-service channels. Mr. Hoyt has served for more than a year in the Division of Passport Control, Department of State, and in the Passport Agency in New York City, and has been acting as passport agent for the past several months. He has thus acquired the desired experience and hi appointment would appear to be in the interest of the public service. 
August 15, 1919. 
In recognition of the services during the war of Capt. J. J. Doyle, of Seattle, Wash., the civil-service regulation prescribing the age limit for examination for inspector of hulls in the Steamboat-Inspection Service is hereby waived in his case. 
August 30, 1919. 
Mr. Pearson Chapman, formerly a topographer in the United States Geological Survey, whose health was broken while in the service of the Government necessi- tating his separation, may be reinstated to the position of topographer in the Geo- logical Survey without regard to the length of his separation from the service. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation of the Secretary of the Interior for this action. 
September 3, 1919. 
Mrs. Clara E. Graves may be appointed to a clerical position in the classified civil service of the Department of Commerce without complying with the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendations of the Secretary of Commerce and 
the Superintendent of the Coast and Geodetic Survey, who state that Mrs. Graves is the widow of Mr. Herbert C. Graves who died while attending an international hydro- aphic conference in England as a representative of this country, and who was the ont of an important division in the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey; that Mr. Graves was a most conscientious and hard working man and that he applied him- self diligently and untiringly to the Government’s interests; that as a result of his death his widow and small children have been left without means of support; that Mrs. Graves is fully competent to perform the duties of the position to which it is proposed to appoint her. For these reasons it is believed that an exception to the rules in her case is warranted in the interest of the service.

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 125 
December 28, 1920. 
Mr. Ernest D. Pickell may be appointed to the position of rural free delivery 
carrier at Huron, S. Dak., without regard to civil-service examination. 
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Postmaster General on 
account of this employee’s faithful and efficient service, and because of the 
difficulty experienced in securing a permanent rural carrier to fill this position. 
His appeintment would be in the interest of the service. He is disqualified 
from taking the required examination on account of his age, he being 52 years 
old. 
January 28, 1921. 
Mrs. Emma V. Morgan may be appointed to a position in the classified service 
in the Department of Labor without reference to the requirements of the civil￾service rules. , 
This order is recommended by the Secretary of Labor, who states that Mrs. 
Morgan is a woman of very unusual ability, efficiency, and reliability. 
February 2, 1921. 
Morris A. Parris may be appointed as clerk to act as confidential secretary 
to the Director of the Bureau of Standards, at $1,800 per annum, without re￾gard to the requirements of the civil-service rules. 
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Director of the Bureau 
of Standards and of the Secretary of Commerce, Mr. Parris having demon￾strated under temporary appointment that he possesses the peculiar qualifica￾tions and experience necessary for the duties of the position. 
February 10, 1921. 
Mr. Arthur Byrd may be appointed a clerk in the Navy Department without 
compliance with the civil-service rules. 
This order is issued in view of the long and efficient service Mr. Byrd has 
rendered in the Navy Department. His duties and responsibilities compare 
favorably with those of many clerks. The position which Mr. Byrd fills has 
grown to one of such importance that if his service were terminated for any 
cause it would be necessary to replace him with a clerk. 
February 12, 1921. 
Mrs. May G. Pollock, of Illinois, may be appointed in the classified service 
without regard to civil-service rules. 
NoTeE.—The commission was not advised of the reasons for the issuance of 
the above order. 
February 18, 1921. 
Miss Margaret Reardon, of virginia, and Mr. Joseph F. Murphy, of New Jer￾sey, may be appointed to positions in the classified service of the Government 
without reference to the civil-service rules. 
Miss Reardon and Mr. Murphy have been employed in the executive office for 
a number of months and have rendered efficient service. 
March 4, 1921. 
Miller W. Gieseking, of Washington, D. C., may be appointed to a clerical posi￾tion in the classified service of the Government without reference to the civil￾service rules. ; 
Mr. Gieseking has been employed in the executive offices for nearly three 
vears and has rendered efficient and faithful service. 
March 5, 1921. 
Mrs. Mabel P. LeRoy, of Michigan, appointed by the Secretary of the Interior 
February 25, 1910, to the position of clerk to sign land patents, is hereby desig￾nated as required by law to sign said patents. 
Note.—The commission was not advised of the reasons for the issuance of 
the above order. 
March 19, 1921. 
Mrs. Mary T. K. McBlair, of the District of Columbia, may be appointed to a 
position in the classified civil service without reference to the civil-service rules. 
Mrs. McBlair has been temporarily employed in the Bureau of Naturalization 
in the Department of Labor, where she has rendered faithful and industrious 
service.

The Executive order of February 2, 1921, placing within the competit ve classi￾fied service the position of examiner of tea is hereby amended to the extent 
of aecording a classified status to Henry F. Brown, who has been hold ng the 
position since 1904. Mr. Brown attained the highest eligible rating in the 
second examination which was held to fill the position, but which was later can￾celed and the position taken out of the classified service. 
April 14, 1921. 
The year limit upon eligibility for reinstatement is waived to permit the re￾instatement of Hugh C. Mitchell as computer in the Coast and Geodetic Sur￾vey of the Department of Commerce. Mr. Mitchell was regularly employed in 
the Coast and Geodetic Survey from August 22, 1898, to December 7, 1911, and 
has since been engaged upon work in the line of his profession. This order is 
issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce in view of Mr. 
Mitchell’s long, faithful, and efficient service and the present need of his serv￾ices. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation in view 
of Mr. Mitchell having originally entered the service through competitive ex￾amination and in view of his having continued to the present time in work 
in, the line of his profession, thereby tending to maintain his efficiency. 
~ April 14, 1921. 
Mrs. Martha Rich Smith may be appointed as clerk at $1,100 per annum in 
the office of headquarters, United States Marine Corps, Washington, D. C., 
without reference to the civil-service rules. 
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Assistant Secretary of 
the Navy, in view of the facts that Mrs. Smith was enrolled in the United 
States Naval Reserve Force during the World War and performed active duty 
in the Navy Department from July 11, 1918, to July 31, 1919, and was given a 
temporary appo:ntment as clerk on August 1, 1919, from which position she 
resigned on June 30, 1920; and that she suffered the loss of her son, Lieut. 
Clarence W. Smith, United. States Marine Corps, in the World War, he being 
killed in action overseas. Lieut. Smith was awarded the Croix de Guerre by 
the French Government for his gallant and conspicuous conduct in action 
against the enemy on the battle field of France. 
The Civil Service Commission was unable to concur in recommending this 
order.

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 129

he is now employed and where he has rendered excellent service. He has been 
promoted twice and is assigned to very important work. 
This order is issued upon recommendation of the Attorney Ceneral, with the 
concurrence of the Civil Service Commission. 
January 12, 1922. 
Mr. Paul Bazaar may be appointed as clerk in the Rochester, N. Y., office 
of the United States Veterans’ Bureau, without examination under the civil 
service rules. 
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Director of the United 
States Veterans’ Bureau. Mr. Bazaar, who suffered the loss of both hands in 
the World War, has by the use of artificial hands become so rehabilitated that 
he can operate a typewriter and satisfactorily perform clerical duties. The 
case being exceptional, the director believes that his appointment would have 
a beneficial psychological effect upon the disabled ex-service men in that vicinity. 
January 25, 1922. 
Mr. Ernest W. Camp may be appointed Chief, Division of Customs, Treasury 
Department, without examination under the civil service rules. 
March 6, 1922. 
Mr. Arthur W. Mueller may be appointed to the position of clerk in the Post 
Office Department without regard to civil service rules and regulations. 
The Postmaster General recommends this order in view of Mr. Mueller’s 
satisfactory service in the Division of Air Mail Service, which service at the 
time of Mr. Mueller’s appointment was not treated as in the classified service. 
The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
March 6, 1922. 
Mrs. Mary Asquith Hughes may be appointed to a clerical position in the 
classified service of the Government without regard to the requirements of the 
civil-service rules. 
Mrs. Hughes, who had some clerical experience prior to her marriage, is the 
widow of William G. Hughes, who was appointed to a position in the Bureau 
of Construction and Repair, Navy Department, on June 9, 1890, and continued 
in the employ of said department under various ratings until he lost his life 
in the Knickerbocker disaster on January 28, 1922, and who was considered 
by his immediate superiors and fellow workers as a most efficient employee. 
March 23, 1922. 
Thomas B. McKaig may be appointed to a permanent position in the classi￾fied service of the Treasury Department without regard to the requirements of 
the civil-service rules. 
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, 
who states that Mr. McKaig has rendered distinguished service as a temporary 
valuation expert in the Valuation Investigation Division; that he has shown 
the highest qualifications for executive administrative responsibilities; and that 
his permanent appointment will be greatly in the interest of the service. 
The Cvil Service Commission did not concur in recommending the order. 
April 22, 1922. 
John M. Masten may be appointed to a position as investigator in the Gen￾eral Accounting Office without compliance with civil-service rules. Mr. Masten 
has had wide and varied experience in investigating work in the Post Office 
Department, and it is believed that in view of his qualifications and experience 
in this line of work it would be in the interest of the service to make this 
appointment. 
April 22, 1922. 
Frank H. Bogardus may be appointed to a position as investigator in the 
General Accounting Office without compliance with civil-service rules. Mr. 
Bogardus has had wide and varied experience as investigator along accounting 
lines. He was temporarily appointed as investigator, on November 16, 1921, in 
the General Accounting Office, and his services have proven entirely satisfactory

WAIVER OF EXAMINATION REQUIREMENT. May 7, 1923. 
The Executive order of May 10, 1921, requiring candidates to take civil service examinations for presidential postmasterships, is hereby waived so as to permit the appointment of Henry M. Stowe to the position of postmaster at Bedford, Va., without 
examination. 
May 7, 1928. 
The Executive order of May 10, 1921, prescribing examinations of applicants for presidential postmasters is hereby waived in so far as it applies to the case of the ostmaster at Falmouth, Mass., in order to permit the reappointment without exam￾ination of George W. Jones. Mr. Jones was appointed postmaster in the Falmouth, Mass., post office October 12, 1889, and has been serving continuously in that capacity since that time. The Civil Service Commission concurs in this recommendation. 
REAPPOINTMENT WITHOUT EXAMINATION. 
WAIVER OF AGE LIMIT. May 11, 1928. 
That part of the Executive order of May 10, 1921, which pertains to the age limit of candidates for the presidential postmastership examinations is hereby waived so as to permit the examination papers of Isaac I. Bargen, candidate for the position of Postimasior at Mountain Lake, Minn., to be rated by the Civil Service Commission. 
e has served as postmaster since 1902. The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this order. 
May 18, 1923. 
That part of the Executive order of May 10, 1921, which pertains to the age limit of candidates for the presidential postmastership examination is hereby waived so as to permit the examination papers of W. W. Copeland, candidate for the position of postmaster at Burlington, Iowa, to be rated by the Civil Service Commission. 
May 28, 1928. 
The papers of the examination of Mr. George W. Sisler for postmaster at Stanwood, lowa, may be rated by the Civil Service Commission, waiving the age limit. Mr. Sisler was postmaster from 1911 to 1917. It is stated that he is at the present time the choice of the majority, if not all, of the business men of the town for the office and that he is very competent. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the Postmaster General in recommend- ing the issuance of this order. 
MISCELLANEOUS ORDER. 
AMENDMENT OF EXECUTIVE ORDER OF JANUARY 17, 1873, PROHIBITING THE HOLDING 
OF FEDERAL AND STATE OFFICES AT THE SAME TIME, 
January 2, 1923. 
The Executive order of January 17, 1873, prohibiting the holding of Federal and State offices at the same time is hereby amended so as to permit the appointment as special agents of persons holding State, territorial, or municipal positions when such action is deemed necessary by the Secretary of Labor to secure a more efficient admin- istration of any law coming within the purview of the Department of Labor. 
ELIGIBILITY FOR REENTRANCE TO THE CLASSIFIED SERVICE FOR A PERIOD OF FIVE 
YEARS FROM MARCH 31, 1922, OF CERTAIN PERSONS SEPARATED FROM THE BUREAU 
OF ENGRAVING AND PRINTING. 
February 14, 1923. 
The following-named persons who were separated from the Bureau of Engraving and Printing are eligible to reenter any part of the classified service in appropriate positions for a period of five years from March 31, 1922, on certificate of the Civil Service Commission: P. J. Farrell, James M. Fisher, George E. Jacobs, Thomas F. Roche, George U. Rose, Adam P. Ruth, Thomas F. Slattery, E. H. Ashworth, Jesse Benjamin, Ralph H. Onappell George C. Cole, William C. Deane, John J. Deviny, B. R. Stickney, Norman Underwood, H. I. Wilson, Benjamin Goldsworthy.

The following-named persons are not eligible for reentrance to the service because they have been retired jupon annuity: Frederick J. Crocker, William C. McKinney, Frank W. Larner, Frank Campbell, Annie E. Bealle, George F.C. Smillie. The reinstatement of Mrs. M. S. Kerfoot, Elizabeth W. Scott, and Nellie Wilding have already been authorized. 
EXEMPTING POSITION OF SHIPPING COMMISSIONER FROM CIVIL-SERVICE REGULATION. 
March 15, 19283. 
The position of{ShippingiCommissioner at the several ports of the United States is hereby exempted from civil-service regulation. Officers of the jNaval Reserve force who bear recommendations from the Secretary of the Navy shall be given priority whenever it is necessary to select new men to these positions. 
POSITIONS OF GUARD IN THE OFFICE OF ,THE SUPERINTENDENT, STATE, WAR, AND NAVY DEPARTMENT BUILDINGS. June 2, 1923. 
Positions of guard in the office of the superintendent, State, War, and Navy Depart» ment Buildings, may, during the remainder of the fiscal year 1923 and during the fiscal year 1924, be filled by the superintendent without compliance with the civil- service law and rules when filled by suitably qualified retired enlisted men from the Army, Navy, or Marine Corps, or retired firemen or policemen of the District of Columbia Government who have been retired therefrom under honorable conditions. The excessive turnover in the guard force, due to inadequate salaries under exist- ing conditions, and the desirability of assigning to the temporary frame buildings as guards men who have had training and experience in the Fire Department indicate the desirability of the exception proposed. It is anticipated that the reclassifica- Hon fel; which becomes effective oo 1, 1924, will take care of the situation after 
at date. 
The Civil Service Commission concurs with the Secretary of State and the Acting Secretaries of War and Navy in recommending this order. 
PERMISSION TO EMPLOYEES LIVING IN BRENTWOOD, MD., TO BECOME CANDIDATES FOR OR HOLD MUNICIPAL OFFICE, June 7, 1923. 
The Executive order of February 14, 1912, as subsequently amended, permitting employees in the executive civil service permanently residing in certain incor- porated municipalities adjacent to the District of Columbia to become candidates for or hold municipal office therein, is hereby further amended so as to include the in- corporated municipality of Brentwood, Md., among those named in the order. May 28, 1928.

MISCELLANEOUS ORDER. 
AMENDMENT OF EXECUTIVE ORDER OF JANUARY 17, 1873, PROHIBITING THE HOLDING 
OF FEDERAL AND STATE OFFICES AT THE SAME TIME, 
January 2, 1923. 
The Executive order of January 17, 1873, prohibiting the holding of Federal and State offices at the same time is hereby amended so as to permit the appointment as special agents of persons holding State, territorial, or municipal positions when such action is deemed necessary by the Secretary of Labor to secure a more efficient admin- istration of any law coming within the purview of the Department of Labor.

AMENDMENT OF FOURTH-CLASS POSTMASTER REGULATIONS
NOT TO BE EXAMINED AFTER REACHING 85 YEARS OF AGE
January 12, 1925. 
On the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission and the Postmaster
General the word "examined" is substituted for the word "appointed" in line 1
of section 7, Regulations Governing the Appointment of Postmasters of the Fourth
Class. As amended section 7 will read:
"7. No person shall be examined under the regulations of November 25, 1912,
as amended, as postmaster of an office of the fourth class where the annual
compensation is as much as $500 after he has reached his sixty-fifth birthday."
ORDERS RELATING TO EXAMINATIONS FOR PRESIDENTIAL POST
OFFICES
WAIVER OF EXAMINATION REQUIREMENT
January 8, 1925. 
Mr. A. H. Bergthold may be appointed postmaster at Weatherford, Okla.,
without regard to the Executive order of May 10, 1921, requiring candidates to
pass a civil-service examination for presidential postmasterships.
This order is issued on recommendation of the Postmaster General, who states
that Mr. Bergthold has been acting postmaster since June 5, 1923, and his service
has been satisfactory.
The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending this order.
WAIVER OF AGE REQUIREMENT
January 10, 1925. 
Mr. Charles C. Kellogg may be admitted to the examination for postmaster at
Detroit without regard to his age.
Mr. Kellogg has been in the classified service since 1895 and, if his promotion
without examination were proposed, his age would not be a bar.
The Civil Service Commission concurs with the Postmaster General in recom￾mending this order.
ORDERS TRANSFERRING BUREAUS AND OFFICES FROM DEPART￾MENT OF THE INTERIOR TO DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE
TRANSFER OF PATENT OFFICE, DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, TO DEPARTMENT
OF COMMERCE
March 17, 1925. 
I, Calvin Coolidge, President of the United States of America, under the
authority conferred upon me by Act of February 14, 1903, entitled "An Act to
establish the Department of Commerce and Labor" (32 Stat. 826), and by virtue
of all other powers thereto me enabling, do hereby transfer from the Department
of the Interior to the Department of Commerce, to be administered under the
supervision of the Secretary of Commerce, the United States Patent Office,
together with all appropriations, the records and all public property of said service
in the District of Columbia or elsewhere, as provided in the Act of February 14,
1903, supra. The transfer above mentioned shall be effective from and including
April 1, 1925.
